  M = ⎣(1+3)/2⎦ = 2,
and one finds
  f(0) = 0 + 1 = 1  (since 0 ≤ 2),

sentence: A key observation is that although the rule “looks different” for n ≤ M and for n > M, one may “hide” the subtraction by thinking modulo a+b.

In fact, if you write f in the form
  f(n) = n + a – (a+b)·χ(n > M)
(where χ(…) is the indicator function), then modulo a+b one always have
  f(n) ≡ n + a  (mod (a+b)).
sentence-category-reason: Rewrites f using an indicator and deduces a congruence relation; theoretical reasoning.

So a necessary condition to have f^k(0)=0 (as an ordinary integer, not just modulo a+b) is that
